title: The Airlock

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 21: Begin with the first checklist item. Everything else is just the next one.*

The pump house smelled of hot oil and cold metal, a scent Kess associated with safety, or perhaps with the specific flavor of holding one's breath for a very long time. The console glowed amber, casting long, soft shadows across the faces of the crew. Tally’s voice came through the speakers, clear and steady, reading the thermal map that shimmered on the main wall like a heat signature made of light. The drum had been slowed by a tenth, a subtle change that made the air feel lighter, less oppressive, as if the ship itself was leaning forward to listen.

Voss stood at Kess’s shoulder, his arms crossed, his ginger beard twitching with the effort of not checking his watch. He looked like a man trying to hold a leak together with his will alone. Pim sat on a crate, his knees drawn up to his chest, holding a stopwatch in one hand and a biscuit in the other. He took a bite, chewed thoughtfully, and then looked at the screen. He had eaten three biscuits already. He seemed to have an unlimited supply, or an unlimited appetite, or perhaps both.

"Thermal map stable," Tally said. "Coolant flow nominal. Pressure within tolerance."

Kess adjusted her headset, the foam pressing against her temples. She looked at Lio, who was standing by the airlock, his face pale and set. He nodded once, a small, sharp movement.

"Checklist ready?" she asked.

"Ready," he said. His voice was calm, but his hands were shaking. She could see the tremor in his fingers, the way they curled and uncurled against the metal frame of the airlock.

Pim raised his stopwatch. "Time zero," he announced, his voice bright and brittle. "Good luck, Lio. I believe in you. Statistically."

Voss uncrossed his arms. "Don't listen to him," he said, his voice gruff but not unkind. "Just close the valve. That's all you have to do. Close the valve, and we're done."

Kess looked at the screen, at the cold spot that looked so small, so insignificant, against the vast, glowing expanse of the radiator wing. It was a tiny imperfection, a hiccup in the machine’s long breath. But she knew, in her bones, that it was the beginning of the end.

"Open the hatch," she said.

The outer hatch groaned, a deep, metallic sound that vibrated through the floor. The stars waited outside, cold and indifferent, ready to take what the ship had to give.
pages.image: Inside a dim, utilitarian pump house, Kess in a green coverall stands at a glowing amber console, Lio in a navy jumpsuit stands by a large airlock door, Chief Voss with a ginger beard watches, and Pim in a red hoodie holds a stopwatch, the air thick with tension and anticipation.

pages.text:
The airlock was a cube of silence, a small, sealed world where the only sound was the hum of the life support and the rapid, rhythmic beat of Lio’s own heart. He stood in the center, his helmet sealed tight, the glass dark and reflective. On his wrist, a small card was attached to his suit, the checklist written in his own careful, precise handwriting. He read the first step aloud, his voice muffled by the helmet, steady and strong.

"Pressure equalized."

Kess listened through the speakers, her eyes closed. She counted the seconds, each one a small, solid stone in a bridge they were building over a chasm. She could hear his breathing, slow and controlled, a steady rhythm that matched the pulse of the ship.

"Suit integrity confirmed," he said. "Tether secured."

Kess opened her eyes. The amber light from the console cast a warm glow on his face, highlighting the tension in his jaw, the fear that lived in the back of his eyes. He was afraid. She knew he was afraid. But he was also ready.

"Three points of contact," she said, her voice soft but firm.

"Clipped," he said.

The outer hatch swung open, a slow, heavy movement that seemed to take an eternity. The stars spilled in, not as a view, but as a presence, a vast, cold, infinite darkness that wrapped around him, holding him, waiting. He stepped out, his boots finding the first rung of the service rail, his hands gripping the cold metal.

Kess watched the camera feed, the image sharp and clear, her heart tightening in her chest. He was small, so small, against the huge, silver expanse of the wing. But he was moving, steady and sure, his movements precise and practiced.

"Moving along the rail," he said. "Heading toward the manifold."

Kess nodded, though he could not see her. She took a breath, a deep, full breath that filled her lungs with the scent of oil and metal, and waited.
pages.image: Lio in a white EVA suit stands at the threshold of an open airlock, the vast starfield visible behind him, his face visible through the helmet, looking calm and determined, Kess's voice echoing in the silence.

pages.text:
The service rail stretched out before him, a thin, silver line that vanished into the dark. Lio moved along it, hand over hand, his tether sliding through the guide rings with a soft, smooth whisper. Below him, the stars did not shine; they simply existed, a cold, static field of light that offered no comfort and no warmth. He felt no pull at all, only the faint drag of the tether, and behind him the whole turning world that held them together.

Kess watched the feed, her eyes tracking his movement, her breath held in her throat. He moved with a grace she had not expected, a fluidity that spoke of years of practice, of hours spent in the zero-g bay, of a mind that had mapped this path a thousand times in her imagination.

"Heading steady," she said, her voice quiet but clear. "Keep your eyes on the manifold. Don't look down. Don't look up. Just look at the valve."

"I see it," he said. "It's right there."

A tear slid down Kess's cheek, a hot, stinging drop she quickly wiped away. She did not care about the tear, or the fear, or the pressure of the ship on her shoulders. She only cared that he was moving, that he was alive, that he was doing what needed to be done.

"Pressure stable," Voss said, his voice rough with emotion. "Flow rate holding."

Pim raised his stopwatch. "Four minutes," he said, his voice high and thin. "He's doing well. I think he's doing very well."

Kess looked at the screen, at the small figure moving along the rail, at the vast, cold, beautiful expanse of space that surrounded him. She thought of the trees, of the apples, of the future that hung in the balance. She thought of the promise she had made, the one she had whispered in the dark, the one she had not dared to speak aloud.

"Keep going," she said. "You're doing good."
pages.image: A view from a helmet camera showing Lio in a white EVA suit moving along a silver rail on the outside of a space station, the vast starfield below, the curve of the ship's drums visible in the distance, the scene bright and clear, filled with wonder and tension.

pages.text:
The valve was a large, red wheel, stark against the silver of the pipe. Lio reached for it, his gloved hand wrapping around the rim. It resisted. He pushed back, muscles straining against the torque, feeling the machine’s stubbornness push right back at him.

"Closing the valve," he said, his voice tight with effort. "One turn. Two turns."

Kess watched the pressure gauge on the console. The needle trembled, then began to fall, a slow, graceful descent that mirrored the relief in her chest. The thermal map on the wall flickered, the cold spot shrinking, dimming, as if the ship itself was sighing.

"Pressure dropping," she said, her voice steady, controlled. "Flow rate decreasing. We're losing the extra percent. On schedule."

Voss leaned forward, his hands gripping the edge of the console. "Half the lights," he said, his voice quiet, almost a whisper. "The ship is dimming."

Kess looked around the pump house. The overhead fluorescents flickered and died, leaving only the amber glow of Tally’s screen to cut through the gloom. The room felt smaller, darker, but also safer, more contained. The ship was settling, adjusting, finding its new balance.

"Valve closed," Lio said, his voice clear and strong. "Isolation complete."

Kess exhaled, a long, slow release that filled the room with the scent of oil and metal. She looked at Pim, who was smiling, his eyes bright, his stopwatch raised in the air.

"Seven minutes," he said. "That’s a record. I think that’s a record."

Voss nodded, his face softening, the tension in his shoulders easing. "Good work, kid," he said, his voice rough with pride. "Good work."

Kess looked at the screen. There was Lio, a small figure standing by the valve, framed by the vast, cold expanse of space. She felt the tension leave her limbs, replaced by a warm, humming vibration in her bones. It was the feeling of a graft taking hold, of a root finding solid ground after a long, precarious journey through the air.

She turned to Voss, then to Pim, who was already scribbling in his notebook, his glowing-soled sneakers tapping a nervous rhythm on the metal floor.

"Seven minutes," Kess repeated, a small smile tugging at the corner of her mouth. "You should write that down. Before you forget."

"I have," Pim said, holding up the notebook. "It’s in the margin. Under 'Valve' and next to 'Record'."

Lio’s face appeared on the screen, flushed and bright. He gave a small, precise wave.

"See you in the airlock," he said.

"See you in the airlock," Kess answered.
pages.image: Inside the pump house, Kess in a green coverall watches a screen showing Lio in a white EVA suit closing a red valve, the lights in the room dimming, Voss with a ginger beard looks on with pride, Pim in a red hoodie smiles holding a stopwatch, the atmosphere tense but hopeful.

pages.text:
Lio moved along the rail again, his movements slower now, more deliberate. He was listening to the ship, to the machine, to the truth that was waiting for him. The manifold joint loomed before him, a large, complex assembly of pipes and valves. It was a knot of metal that had held the ship together for decades. He reached out, his gloved hand touching the cold surface. He felt the vibrations, the hum, the life that pulsed beneath the skin of the alloy.

Then he saw it.

A hairline crack, thin and dark, ran along the weld. It was a scar that the camera had missed and the thermal map had not revealed. It was small, so small, but it was there. It was a flaw in the perfection, a crack in the promise.

"Kess," he said, his voice small, quiet, barely audible over the hum of the ship. "It's worse than the camera showed."

Kess leaned forward, her breath catching in her throat. She looked at the screen, at the small figure, at the manifold, at the crack that was so thin and insignificant that it was almost invisible.

"The pipe," she said, her voice tight, controlled. "Say again the length of the crack."

Voss swore, a low, gentle sound that echoed in the silence of the pump house. He looked at Kess, his eyes wide, his face pale. The plan had just changed. The simple, elegant solution they had worked for, the one that was supposed to save the ship, was no longer enough.

Kess looked at the screen, at the crack, at Lio, at the stars that waited outside. She felt the burden of the vessel, the burden of the years ahead, the burden of the truth. She took a breath, a deep, full breath, and waited for him to answer.
pages.image: Lio in a white EVA suit stands before a complex manifold joint on the outside of a space station, his face visible through the helmet, looking concerned and serious, a thin crack visible on the metal pipe, the starfield in the background, the scene tense and urgent.
